claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr/V-rich precipitates under irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 undergoes modest or measurable irradiation hardening.
Adding 1–2 at.% Hf during synthesis will promote Hf segregation to grain boundaries.
Approximately 1050 K is a fusion-relevant irradiation temperature at which defect mobility and grain-boundary processes are active.
Hf-enriched grain-boundary layers act as barriers to solute diffusion.
Hf-enriched grain boundaries are preferential sites for irradiation-defect recombination.
Grain-boundary Hf stabilizes the boundary structure and lowers the free-energy cost associated with Cr and V redistribution.
Hf segregation reduces the thermodynamic driving force for Cr/V-rich precipitation.
Enhanced defect recombination at Hf-enriched boundaries counteracts radiation-induced clustering that leads to precipitation.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Hf-modified alloy will have a lower density of Cr/V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Hf-modified alloy will have smaller Cr/V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening or show only a slight increase in hardening.
Adding Hf will improve microstructural stability and make the alloy more suitable for practical bulk fabrication.
Hf segregation kinetics remain effective near 1050 K and approximately 8 dpa.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says Hf will prevent precipitation, whereas the predicted outcome only requires lower precipitate density and size, and the falsification rule permits any reduction relative to the control. Nonzero precipitation could therefore satisfy the prediction while contradicting the stronger prevention claim.
